title: Our Changing Planet: What the Science Says
paragraphs: The Earth's climate has always changed. In the four and a half billion years of the planet's history, temperatures have fluctuated, ice ages have come and gone, and seas have risen and fallen by hundreds of metres. What is happening now is different, and the difference is the speed. The changes that are currently being recorded across the planet are occurring at a rate that has not been seen in the geological record for at least 65 million years.

The primary driver is the increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide. When fossil fuels are burned — coal in power stations, oil in cars, gas in homes — carbon that was stored underground for millions of years is released into the atmosphere in a matter of decades. This carbon traps heat that would otherwise escape into space. The planet warms. The oceans absorb much of this heat, which causes water to expand and ice to melt. Sea levels rise.

In Kazakhstan, the effects are already being recorded. The Aral Sea — once the fourth-largest lake in the world — was drained by Soviet-era irrigation projects over the second half of the twentieth century. Today it has been reduced to a fraction of its original size, and the land around it has been turned into a salt desert. The nearby communities have been affected by dust storms, declining fish stocks, and rising rates of respiratory disease.

The Tian Shan mountains, which form part of Kazakhstan's southern and eastern border, have been losing glacier mass at an accelerating rate. The glaciers have retreated significantly over the past fifty years. These glaciers are a critical source of fresh water for the region — when they are gone, the rivers they feed will be dramatically reduced.

Not everything that is happening can be attributed to human activity. The climate has natural cycles of variation. But the scientific consensus — supported by data from thousands of researchers across dozens of countries — is clear: the current warming trend has been accelerated significantly by human activity, and it will continue unless emissions are dramatically reduced.

What can be done? The technologies that are needed to decarbonise the global economy largely exist. Solar and wind power are being deployed at unprecedented scale. Electric vehicles are being produced in growing numbers. Carbon capture is being researched and piloted. The question is not whether the solutions exist — it is whether they will be implemented quickly enough to make a difference.

For students studying in Kazakhstan in 2026, these are not abstract problems. They are the conditions of the world you will work in. Whether you study ecology, engineering, medicine, or economics, the changing environment will affect your field. Understanding the science is not optional. It is the literacy of the twenty-first century.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Do you think Kazakhstan is doing enough on climate? I read that the Aral Sea is just a fraction of what it was.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: It's heartbreaking. That was done decades ago — bad decisions were made and now entire communities are affected.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: The glacier retreat is also alarming. Those are our water sources.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: I know. In my ecology lectures we've been told that some rivers might lose 40% of their flow within a generation.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Is technology enough? Or do habits need to change?

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: Both. But I think the structures have to change — energy systems, transport, agriculture.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: It feels overwhelming sometimes. Like, what can one student do?

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: Understand the problem deeply. Then work on part of it. That's where it starts.

keyPhrases.context: "Not seen in the geological record for 65 million years." — physical evidence in rock layers.
"The increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide." — carbon in the air.
"When fossil fuels are burned." — coal, oil, gas from prehistoric organisms.
"The scientific consensus is clear." = agreement among the scientific community.
"Decarbonise the global economy." = remove carbon from energy and industry.
"Deployed at unprecedented scale." = at a scale never seen before.
"Rising rates of respiratory disease." — illnesses affecting breathing.
"Carbon capture is being researched." = technology to remove CO₂ from the air.

Solar power is being deployed at unprecedented scale.

vocab.definition: to move back from a position; to withdraw
vocab.example: The glaciers have retreated significantly over fifty years.

vocab.definition: to use or put into action, especially on a large scale
vocab.example: Solar and wind power are being deployed at unprecedented scale.
